name: Solitary fibrous tumour of the pleura

clinicalPearls: A mesenchymal tumour usually arising from the visceral pleura, most often benign but with a minority behaving in a malignant fashion
Distinct from diffuse malignant mesothelioma and not related to asbestos exposure
Frequently asymptomatic and found incidentally as a well-defined, sometimes pedunculated pleural-based mass
Large tumours may cause cough, chest discomfort, or breathlessness through local mass effect
Associated paraneoplastic syndromes include hypertrophic osteoarthropathy and, classically, hypoglycaemia from tumour secretion of insulin-like growth factor (Doege-Potter syndrome)
Characterised molecularly by the NAB2-STAT6 gene fusion, with nuclear STAT6 expression on immunohistochemistry
Complete surgical resection is the treatment of choice and is usually curative for benign lesions
Because late or malignant recurrence can occur, prolonged imaging follow-up after resection is advised
reference.pathophysiology: The tumour arises from CD34-positive fibroblast-like mesenchymal cells of the submesothelial pleura rather than from mesothelial cells themselves. A recurrent intrachromosomal NAB2-STAT6 gene fusion is the defining molecular event, driving cell proliferation and producing the nuclear STAT6 immunopositivity used diagnostically. Most tumours grow slowly as a circumscribed, often pedunculated mass and remain benign, but a subset show high mitotic activity, necrosis, and infiltrative growth that predict malignant behaviour. Some tumours secrete an incompletely processed insulin-like growth factor that produces refractory hypoglycaemia, the basis of Doege-Potter syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Peripheral bronchial carcinoma abutting the pleura
Neurogenic tumour of the chest wall or mediastinum
Localised organising pleural effusion or fibrous plaque
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax to characterise the mass and its pleural origin
MRI to assess a pedunculated stalk and relationship to adjacent structures
Image-guided or surgical biopsy with immunohistochemistry, including STAT6 and CD34
PET-CT where malignant behaviour or metastasis is suspected
Blood glucose monitoring and relevant hormonal studies if paraneoplastic hypoglycaemia is suspected
redFlags: Rapid enlargement or a large tumour with invasive features on imaging
Recurrent symptomatic hypoglycaemia indicating a paraneoplastic effect
Histological features of high mitotic count, necrosis, or infiltration
reference.prognosis: Benign, completely resected tumours have an excellent outlook, whereas malignant or incompletely excised lesions may recur locally or metastasise, so long-term surveillance is recommended.
pitfalls: Confusing a solitary fibrous tumour with diffuse malignant mesothelioma and mislabelling the prognosis
Assuming all such tumours are benign and omitting long-term follow-up
Overlooking paraneoplastic hypoglycaemia as the cause of unexplained low glucose
Incomplete resection leaving a stalk or margin that predisposes to recurrence
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
management: Complete surgical resection with clear margins is the mainstay and is curative for benign, well-circumscribed tumours
Correction of paraneoplastic hypoglycaemia (Doege-Potter syndrome) with glucose support, definitive control coming from tumour removal
Histological and molecular confirmation with STAT6 and CD34 immunohistochemistry to guide risk stratification
Radiotherapy or systemic therapy considered for malignant, unresectable or incompletely excised tumours
Long-term imaging surveillance for local recurrence or metastasis, particularly with high-mitotic-index or malignant lesions
Thoracic surgical and oncology multidisciplinary management
